A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original video-model training experiments, simulated physical-motion evaluations and human assessments of combinatorial generalization, including Figure 3 and Table 2.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds experiments involving Stable Video Diffusion, an alternative VAE and attribute-comparison controls.

M1.justification: The primary frozen VAE, DiT architecture, 3D RoPE, frame-and-mask conditioning and diffusion objective remain unchanged. The alternative VAE and Stable Video Diffusion additions are comparison and robustness experiments, rather than revisions to the primary method.

E1.justification: Both versions study the same Box2D motion and collision tasks, PHYRE combinatorial scenarios and attribute-composition problems. The added experiments reuse this coverage with different models, controls or within-task sampling; no new benchmark, domain or task is introduced.

E2.justification: V2 Appendix D.2 and Table 4 add fine-tuned Stable Video Diffusion and its VAE-reconstruction reference alongside DiT-B and ground truth for uniform motion. This is a targeted comparator extension; the original scaling, combinatorial and multimodal comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce binary velocity and size endpoints, red-only controls without attribute conflicts, an alternative frozen VAE and 300K-step SVD fine-tuning. The original continuous comparisons remain in Appendix E.2, and the main experiments retain their stated budgets, splits and metrics.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands checks of the proposed generalization mechanism: binary attribute comparisons, controls without attribute conflicts, alternative-VAE robustness and pretrained-SVD evaluation. It also adds a training-loss curve and further physical-failure cases. V1's multimodal, ring-versus-ball and composition-failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies that abnormal rates are averaged across ten evaluators who independently review the videos; v1 leaves this aggregation unspecified. This clarifies statistical estimation of the human score, without establishing additional evaluations or adding training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The main scaling results and Tables 2–3 are retained, but supplementary outcomes expand substantially. Table 4 newly reports SVD fine-tuning ID/OOD errors of 0.0505/0.9081; Section 5.3 reports color preservation with size transformation across 202 binary-comparison cases. Alternative-VAE results, no-conflict controls and eight additional failure examples provide further new findings, rather than improvements to retained scores.

T1.justification: The physical-state formulation, physical-coherence loss and diffusion equations remain substantively unchanged. The added discussions of interpolation, pretraining and generalization do not introduce mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: Both abstracts and conclusions retain the same central claims: scaling helps in-distribution and combinatorial generalization but fails for extrapolation; predictions exhibit case-based behavior and the same attribute-priority ordering. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for excluding velocity metrics in complex scenes, interprets the attribute controls and alternative-model results, discusses pretraining contamination and domain mismatch, and expands implications for robotics data diversity. Existing limitations involving visual ambiguity and retrieval-based failures remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly supplies the learning rate, cosine schedule, AdamW parameters, weight decay and default augmentation. Appendix C.2 documents evaluation sample counts, ten raters, aggregation and exact judging instructions, filling substantial reproducibility gaps. Conversely, v1's premature-exit filtering statement is omitted; this omission does not establish that preprocessing changed.

R1.justification: V2 adds positioning against physical-video evaluations such as VideoPhy and T2V-CompBench, broader video benchmarks, physics-guided generation and pretrained video models. New Appendix F explicitly distinguishes the contribution from general ID/OOD research, substantially expanding the earlier related-work discussion.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the appendix into sections A–G with a contents page, groups model documentation, and moves continuous attribute comparisons out of the main analysis. It also revises section titles, expands evaluation explanations and the conclusion/discussion, and edits prose throughout.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column conference layout, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays. V1 Figure 9 becomes v2 Figure 14, while a new binary-comparison Figure 9, robustness and control plots, a loss curve, additional failure panels and Table 4 are added.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v2 better supports its existing conclusions through targeted model comparisons and attribute controls, while substantially clarifying training and human-evaluation procedures. These gains improve credibility and reproducibility. Their impact is tempered by limited comparative scope and a new Figure 12 inconsistency: the second panel is described as color versus velocity but has radius axes, weakening that robustness evidence.
